subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Sunk Cost Fallacy: Throwing Good After Bad
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Sunk Cost Fallacy: Throwing Good After Bad usable.

hook.text: You're 90 minutes into a terrible movie. You stay because you 'already paid for the ticket.' That's a trap.

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy: continuing something because of what you've already invested, even when quitting is better.

discovery.text: Rationally, past costs are irrelevant. Only future costs and benefits should drive decisions.

twist.text: The Concorde jet cost $2 billion to develop. Both governments knew it would lose money but couldn't stop.

climax.text: Sunk cost thinking traps relationships, careers, wars, and business projects. The cure: ask 'Would I start this today?'

punchline.text: If you wouldn't start it today, stop it today.

quiz.question: What drives the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Inability to let go of past investments

details.summary: The sunk cost fallacy is continuing an endeavor because of previously invested resources that cannot be recovered. Rational decisions should consider only future costs and benefits, ignoring irrecoverable past investments.
details.whyItMatters: Sunk cost thinking keeps people in failing projects, bad movies, and losing investments. Learning to cut losses saves time, money, and energy.
takeaways: Past costs cannot be recovered and should not influence future decisions
Emotional attachment to investment drives the fallacy
Asking 'Would I start this today?' exposes sunk cost traps

faq.question: What is a common everyday example of the sunk cost fallacy?
faq.answer: Finishing a terrible movie because you paid for the ticket. The ticket money is gone regardless. The rational choice is to leave and spend your remaining time on something you enjoy.

faq.question: Why is the sunk cost fallacy so difficult to overcome emotionally?
faq.answer: Abandoning an investment feels like making the loss real and admitting a mistake. Loss aversion and identity protection make it psychologically easier to keep investing than to accept the loss.
